mcqs.question: Why do most feedback tools hide other interviewers' notes from you until you've submitted your own?
options: Because the tool can only display one interviewer's notes at a time for technical reasons
To prevent anchoring — so your written feedback isn't influenced by what an earlier interviewer already said
To keep candidate feedback confidential from the candidate only, not from other interviewers
Because company policy requires feedback to be submitted within one hour of the interview
mcqs.explanation: Hiding others' notes until you submit your own is a deliberate anti-anchoring measure, so each interviewer's assessment stays independent before the panel reconciles them. It isn't a technical display limitation, isn't specifically about candidate confidentiality, and isn't a submission-deadline rule.

mcqs.question: Why does a contradiction between two tellings of the same story typically hurt a candidate more than one mediocre answer?
options: Interviewers are required to automatically fail any candidate who is flagged as inconsistent
A mediocre answer is never actually noted in feedback, so it has no real cost at all
Contradictions only matter if they're caught by the same interviewer in the same round
A contradiction is a trust signal that casts doubt on every other story, not just a competency signal limited to one round
mcqs.explanation: A weak answer costs points on one competency in one round; a contradiction undermines the credibility of everything else you said, which is why hiring committees treat it as a trust problem rather than a scoring problem. There's no automatic-fail rule, mediocre answers do get noted, and the whole point is that contradictions get caught across rounds, not just within one.

mcqs.question: Two interviewers in the same loop ask you the same conflict question. What's the safest approach?
options: Retell your strongest story consistently, or use a comparably strong second story if you have one tagged for that competency
Always switch to a different story the second time, regardless of its strength, to avoid appearing repetitive
Decline to answer the second time and explain you already covered it in an earlier round
Combine both potential stories into one long answer to show more range
mcqs.explanation: Repeating your best story consistently is safer than reaching for a weaker one just to seem non-repetitive; a genuinely strong second story is also fine since it adds a data point. Declining to answer wastes a scoring opportunity, and combining two stories into one usually just produces a rambling, unfocused answer.

mcqs.question: When two interviewers disagree on a candidate's score during a debrief, what typically resolves the disagreement?
options: A simple majority vote among all interviewers in the loop, regardless of the specifics discussed
Whichever interviewer has more seniority automatically overrides the other's score
Discussion around concrete, specific evidence each interviewer can point to from the actual session
The disagreement is left unresolved and the candidate is automatically rejected
mcqs.explanation: Debrief disagreements typically resolve around specific, verifiable evidence one side can cite, not a raw vote, a seniority override, or an automatic rejection — which is exactly why a story with concrete, checkable detail survives that discussion better than a vague one.

mcqs.question: A candidate feels their round-one story could sound more impressive, and tells a punched-up version — larger scope, better outcome — to a later interviewer. What's the risk?
options: None — interviewers never compare notes on the specific content of stories
The inflated details are exactly what a later cross-check against the written round-one feedback would catch, risking a flagged inconsistency
The interviewer will assume the candidate has two genuinely different stories and score both positively
Punching up a story is standard practice and expected by every interviewer
mcqs.explanation: Written feedback captures specific story details, and a later punched-up retelling is precisely the kind of detail a cross-check flags as inconsistent, which damages trust more than a modestly-told original story ever would. Interviewers do compare notes, a later interviewer won't assume two separate stories, and punching up is a real risk, not standard or expected practice.
